notes: Large test-case judgment on contractor contribution and CHA settlements; headline apportionment and scheme conclusions are clear though individual claim findings are voluminous.

enrichment.short_title: DTI contribution claim against mining contractors for respiratory disease
key_facts: The DTI inherited British Coal's liabilities after Griffiths v British Coal Corporation established widespread respiratory disease among miners.
British Coal employed contractors from the late 1950s to 1994 for underground tunnelling and mine development work affecting thousands of men.
The DTI sought contribution or contractual indemnity from AMEC and other contractors for settlements under the Coal Health Claims administrative scheme.
Sample lead claims were tried to test apportionment, medical assessment, indemnity clauses, and the reasonableness of CHA awards.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Test-case trial on the DTI's contribution and indemnity claims against mining contractors following the Griffiths litigation.
enrichment.outcome: DTI largely succeeded; CHA awards held reasonable and binding, indemnity clauses enforceable, and liability for contractors' men's respiratory damage apportioned 70% to British Coal and 30% to contractors.
enrichment.ratio: Contractors could not rely on British Coal to police dust suppression and owed independent duties of care to their employees; CHA settlements are reasonable bases for contribution claims and contractual indemnities bite to the extent contractor negligence caused the loss.
legal_issues: Whether DTI could recover contribution or contractual indemnity from mining contractors
Apportionment of liability between British Coal and contractors for dust-related respiratory disease
Whether Coal Health Claims scheme awards were reasonable settlements
Enforceability of contractual indemnity clauses in mining contracts
Medical assessment and diagnosis of COPD, asthma and related conditions in sample claims
linked_authorities: Griffiths and Others v British Coal Corporation [1998]

confidence.notes: Core apportionment, CHA, and indemnity conclusions at the end of the judgment are explicit. Individual claimant medical findings are extensive and not fully summarised here.

notes: Short immigration permission judgment; domestic violence concession policy and Danaie distinction are clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Domestic violence concession immigration permission refused
key_facts: An Indian national entered the UK as a dependent spouse but left the matrimonial home after alleged domestic violence.
An adjudicator found she had been assaulted and recommended reconsideration under the domestic violence concession.
The Secretary of State refused indefinite leave because she lacked an injunction, conviction, or police caution as the policy required.
The applicant argued the Secretary of State fettered discretion, treated like cases differently, and must follow the adjudicator.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to apply for judicial review of a refusal to grant indefinite leave under the domestic violence concession.
enrichment.ratio: The domestic violence concession is a tightly drawn discretionary policy whose formal evidential requirements the Secretary of State may lawfully apply; an adjudicator's view on a concession outside the immigration rules is not a binding determination displacing the Secretary of State's decision.
legal_issues: Whether the Secretary of State unlawfully fettered discretion by requiring formal domestic violence documentation
Whether inconsistent treatment of a similarly situated applicant rendered the decision unlawful
Whether the Secretary of State was bound to follow the adjudicator's findings on the concession
index_terms: Secretary of State for the Home Department v Danaie
linked_authorities: Secretary of State for the Home Department v Danaie [1998] Imm AR 84

confidence.notes: Policy terms, three rejected grounds, and outcome are all explicit in a short judgment.

notes: Detailed agricultural wages JR; exclusion of mushrooms held unlawful under domestic and ECHR grounds though relief was deferred.

enrichment.short_title: Mushroom pickers excluded from manual harvest worker rate
key_facts: Middlebrook, the UK's largest mushroom producer, challenged the Agricultural Wages Order 2003 excluding mushroom harvesters from the lower Manual Harvest Worker rate.
The Board excluded mushrooms after employer representations that mushroom pickers were uniquely skilled year-round workers, later shown to be inaccurate.
Eight mushroom growers objected that their largely agency-based workforce was comparable to other manual harvesters.
At the confirmation meeting the Board deferred reconsideration and did not properly address the objections before making the order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Agricultural Wages Order 2003, including a late amendment raising procedural unfairness grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Claim upheld on merits; exclusion of mushroom pickers held Wednesbury unreasonable and contrary to Article 14 read with A1P1, but remedy deferred for further submissions.
enrichment.ratio: The Board failed lawfully to consider objections and had no objective justification for excluding mushroom pickers from the Manual Harvest Worker category; non-seasonality and unsupported skill assumptions could not justify discriminatory treatment of mushroom growers.
legal_issues: Whether exclusion of mushrooms from the Manual Harvest Worker definition was discriminatory and Wednesbury unreasonable
Whether the Board properly considered objections under Schedule 4 to the Agricultural Wages Act 1948
Whether minimum wage regulation falls within the ambit of A1P1 for Article 14 purposes
What remedy should follow partial invalidity of the order
linked_authorities: Carson and Reynolds v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2003] EWCA Civ 797
R (Hooper) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2003] EWCA Civ 813

confidence.notes: Substantive unlawfulness findings are detailed and clear. Final relief was expressly deferred.

notes: Road Traffic Act 1988 s151(8) appeal; permission and capacity grounds analysed with clear dismissal.

enrichment.short_title: Insurer recovery from owner who permitted uninsured son to drive
key_facts: National Insurance Guarantee Corporation paid about £189,000 after Robert Moore caused a road accident while driving his father's Toyota Carina.
Robert was uninsured because he lacked a valid licence and drove a 1760cc car for pleasure when the policy restricted pleasure use to 1600cc vehicles.
The father honestly believed his son held a valid licence and permitted the use of the vehicle.
The insurer sought recovery from the father under section 151(8) as a person who permitted use of the vehicle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment and a deputy High Court judge's dismissal of the father's appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; father liable under section 151(8) for permitting uninsured use on both licence and engine capacity grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Permitted in section 151(8) should be construed consistently with section 143(1)(b); a permission given on an honest mistaken belief, including one induced by misrepresentation, remains permission, whereas only an expressly conditional permission unfulfilled is not.
legal_issues: Meaning of caused or permitted in section 151(8) of the Road Traffic Act 1988
Whether misrepresentation by the driver negates permission
Whether conditional permission doctrine applies in civil recovery proceedings
Whether the engine capacity ground survived if the licence ground failed

confidence.notes: Statutory construction, authorities, and appeal outcome are directly addressed.

notes: Complex option agreement construction appeal; Milton Lane Allowance analysis and apportionment conclusion are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Portsmouth FC option price and Milton Lane Allowance
key_facts: Portsmouth City Football Club held an option to buy stadium land from Sellar Properties subject to a Milton Lane Allowance reducing price by £1,100,000 minus X.
X was defined by reference to Council consideration for consent to the spine road crossing Milton Lane.
Sellar paid Portsmouth City Council £4.255 million for Barwood land and a Milton Lane strip but the Council refused to apportion the price.
The judge held consent meant only highway authority consent, making X nil and the purchase price £900,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Part 8 declaration on the purchase price payable under an option and supplemental agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Milton Lane Allowance held nil after apportionment but for different reasons, so purchase price is £2,000,000.
enrichment.ratio: Consent in the Milton Lane Allowance formula includes the cost of acquiring the Council's landowner interests needed to cross Milton Lane, not merely highway authority permission; where no specific sum is identified the court may apportion a combined purchase price between the relevant land parcels.
legal_issues: Construction of the Milton Lane Allowance and X in the option agreement
Whether consent included land acquisition as well as highway authority approval
How to ascertain X when the Council refused to apportion consideration
Whether Sellar breached a joint negotiation obligation under clause 13
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896
Antaios Compania Naviera SA v Salen Rederierna AB [1985] AC 191

notes: Clinical negligence ultrasound claim; liability finding and termination counterfactual are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Failure to diagnose cloacal exstrophy on antenatal ultrasound
key_facts: Miss P's fourth pregnancy was referred to Leeds after an exomphalos was seen without a bladder on an earlier scan.
Sonographers at Leeds twice reported visualisation of a bladder when none was present, missing likely cloacal exstrophy.
Cloacal exstrophy is far more serious than a standalone exomphalos and would have supported termination counselling.
The claimant said she would have terminated had the correct diagnosis been communicated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of a clinical negligence claim for wrongful birth arising from antenatal ultrasound care.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for the claimant on liability; damages to be assessed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tertiary referral was made because an exomphalos was seen without a bladder, reasonable care required persistent checks, including filling/emptying observations and Doppler use, before reporting a bladder; mistaken visualisation on that focused scan was negligent.
legal_issues: Whether Leeds sonographers breached the duty of care in antenatal ultrasound scanning
Whether absent bladder with exomphalos should have raised cloacal exstrophy
What diagnostic steps were required on a focused tertiary referral scan
Whether the claimant would have terminated the pregnancy if correctly diagnosed

confidence.notes: Liability decision, medical background, and termination finding are clearly reasoned.

notes: Tri-partite brokerage agreement appeal; designated account clause construction and order reformulation are central and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Insurance brokerage split and designated bank account clause
key_facts: Aon, DAR International and Mr Sfeir agreed a 60/40 revenue split on Saudi Arabian Airlines business in a letter dated 13 November 1998.
Payments to DAR and FNS were to be made pro rata immediately upon receipt into a designated bank account to be agreed.
No designated account was agreed and Aon paid commissions to Mr Sfeir alone after the parties fell out.
DAR sued Aon for its share, including 75% of the 60% split agreed between DAR and Sfeir.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a mercantile judge's decision that Aon was bound to pay DAR under the November 1998 agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on the designated account issue, but allowed to reformulate the order as declaratory and remit outstanding quantum and threshold issues.
enrichment.ratio: The agreement required payment into a jointly agreed designated bank account and impliedly prohibited payment to one joint venturer alone; absent such an account Aon was not entitled to pay out unilaterally to Mr Sfeir.
legal_issues: Whether DAR provided valid consideration for the brokerage agreement
Whether payment to one joint creditor satisfied Aon's obligation
Construction of the designated bank account clause
Whether Aon remained liable in damages for paying Mr Sfeir alone
linked_authorities: Catlin v Cyprus Finance Corporation (London) Ltd [1983] 1 QB 759

notes: Telecom mast prior-approval JR; PDE timing and Wednesbury challenge to late non-decision clearly rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Mobile phone mast prior approval judicial review

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995

key_facts: O2 erected a telecommunications mast outside the applicant's home in Gerrards Cross under permitted development rights.
The developer applied for a prior approval determination but the council did not respond within the 56-day period, after which development could lawfully begin.
Four days after the mast was erected the council decided prior approval was not required.
The applicant sought judicial review of that late decision and argued consultation failures invalidated the permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a local planning authority's prior approval determination on a permitted development telecommunications mast.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no remedy granted because the late decision would not have differed and was not shown Wednesbury unreasonable.
enrichment.ratio: Under Part 24 of the 1995 Order, permitted development may proceed once the 56-day period expires without a prior approval requirement; failure to consult within that period does not invalidate the underlying permission, and a late non-decision cannot be quashed without proof of Wednesbury unreasonableness and resulting prejudice.
legal_issues: Effect of expiry of the 56-day prior approval period under the Permitted Development Order
Whether consultation failures invalidated deemed planning permission
Whether the council's late decision that prior approval was not required was Wednesbury unreasonable
Availability of alternative remedies for neighbour representations
index_terms: R v Staffordshire Moorlands DC ex parte Bartlam
linked_authorities: R v Staffordshire Moorlands District Council ex parte Bartlam (1998) 77 PCR 210
Phillips v First Secretary of State [2003] EWCA 2415

notes: Section 33 asbestos limitation appeal; Court of Appeal's reversal of the judge's discretion is detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Asbestos pleural plaques limitation and section 33 discretion
key_facts: The claimant developed asbestos-related pleural thickening diagnosed in 1991 and was told he could bring a civil claim but chose not to sue.
In 1999 medical correspondence first used the term pleural plaques, which the claimant understood as worsening scarring.
Proceedings against Sheffield City Council were not issued until May 2003, well after the limitation period.
The county court judge disapplied limitation under section 33, but Finnegan had already settled on provisional terms.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court decision on a preliminary limitation issue under section 33 of the Limitation Act 1980.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; section 33 discretion should not have been exercised and the claim against the council cannot proceed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant had significant injury and knowledge of a viable claim from 1991 but deliberately did not sue, a later lay misunderstanding that pleural plaques meant deterioration does not justify disapplying limitation twelve years later; long delay and prejudice to contribution proceedings weigh heavily against section 33 relief.
legal_issues: Date of knowledge under sections 11 and 14 of the Limitation Act 1980
Whether pleural plaques materially changed the claimant's medical or legal position
Exercise of discretion under section 33
Prejudice to defendants in contribution proceedings caused by delay
linked_authorities: Forbes v Wandsworth Health Authority [1997] QB 402
Nash v Eli Lilly & Co [1993] 1 WLR 782
Coad v Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Health Authority [1997] 8 Med LR 154

confidence.notes: Limitation findings, section 33 analysis, and appeal outcome are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Case management appeal in planning JR; Sullivan J directions and listing conflict clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Harlow shopping centre JR listing and case management
key_facts: Mr Ghadami, a trader affected by a major Harlow shopping centre redevelopment, sought judicial review of a September 2003 planning committee resolution.
Sullivan J granted rolled-up permission and directed preparation of a core bundle and skeleton arguments before listing.
The case was listed for 23 June 2004 without regard to those directions and before the claimant's preferred leading counsel was available.
Collins J refused to vacate the fixture, but the Court of Appeal found the timetable incompatible with Sullivan J's order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a case management refusal to vacate the hearing date in rolled-up planning judicial review proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; hearing relisted to 6 and 7 July 2004 with directions for core bundle and skeleton arguments.
enrichment.ratio: A hearing date fixed without regard to prior directions requiring a core bundle and skeleton arguments was inappropriate; where tight timetabling prevents fair preparation the court should adjourn even in case management decisions, especially when junior counsel can represent a party whose leader is unavailable.
legal_issues: Whether the court should vacate an administratively fixed hearing date
Effect of Sullivan J's directions on listing and preparation
Appropriate case management where counsel of choice is unavailable
Preparation requirements for complex planning judicial review

confidence.notes: Procedural history, grounds of appeal, and revised listing directions are clearly set out.
